title: Concurrent orchestration
summary: Several agents run on the same input at the same time, then an aggregator combines their answers. Latency is about the slowest agent. Cost is the sum.
useIf: You want independent perspectives, an ensemble or voting, and the agents do not need each other's output.
avoidIf: Agents depend on one another, or you cannot afford multiplied token cost for a small quality gain.

explain.md: Build with `ConcurrentBuilder(participants=[...]).build()` (Python) or `AgentWorkflowBuilder.BuildConcurrent(agents)` (.NET). Participants are agents or executors. Under the hood this is a fan-out to all participants, a barrier, and a fan-in to an aggregator. The **default aggregator** returns one `AgentResponse` containing **one assistant message per participant**. Replace it with a callback via `.with_aggregator(fn)`, for example to ask a summarizer agent to merge the answers. Only the aggregator's output is terminal unless you set `intermediate_output_from` [[tr24]].

explain.title: Latency and cost of a concurrent run
explain.expr: latency ~ max(agent latencies) + aggregator latency;  cost ~ sum(agent costs) + aggregator cost

vars.v: Default is free (concatenation); a summarizer agent adds a model call

explain.example: Three agents at 4, 5 and 9 seconds plus a 3 second summarizer: about 9 + 3 = 12 seconds, versus 21 seconds if run in sequence. Token cost is three full agent runs plus the summarizer.

explain.md: **How to use it well.** Participants can be agents or custom executors, so a rules-based check can run beside model reviewers. Give each participant a distinct role and instruction, otherwise you pay for several near-identical answers. Treat the aggregator as a design decision: concatenation leaves reconciliation to the reader, a summarizer agent adds a model call, and a voting function is free but needs comparable answers. In a graph, concurrency comes from the fan-out edge and the superstep barrier, so the checkpoint after the step contains all participants' results [[tr24]] [[tr14]].

explain.title: Fan-out, barrier, fan-in
explain.alt: The input fans out to three agents that run at the same time; a barrier waits for all of them; an aggregator produces the output.

blocks.code:
async def summarize(results: list[AgentExecutorResponse]) -> str:
    parts = [f'{r.executor_id}:\n{r.agent_response.messages[-1].text}' for r in results]
    reply = await summarizer.run('\n\n'.join(parts))
    return reply.messages[-1].text

workflow = (ConcurrentBuilder(participants=[researcher, marketer, legal])
            .with_aggregator(summarize)
            .build())
async for event in workflow.run('We launch a budget eBike.', stream=True):
    if event.type == 'output':
        print(event.data)

whereToUse: Multi-perspective review: security, legal and cost reviewers on the same change
Ensembles and voting where disagreement is a signal
Fast multi-source research: each agent queries a different corpus
Latency-sensitive fan-out where the sequential sum would be too slow

use: Participants are independent and can share the same input
Wall-clock time matters more than token cost
You can write a sensible aggregator (merge, vote, rank)
avoid: One participant needs another's output: use sequential
Rate limits or quotas are tight: parallel calls spike TPM and RPM
The aggregator would concatenate unrelated answers that a user then has to reconcile
flips: Quota or budget is tight: run fewer participants, or serialise the expensive ones
Agents should challenge each other over rounds: move to group chat

pitfalls.symptom: A 429 rate-limit error appears only when the orchestration runs
pitfalls.cause: All participants call the model at the same time
pitfalls.fix: Add retry with backoff in the chat client, or stagger and cap parallel participants

pitfalls.symptom: Final output shows only one combined message and not each agent's
pitfalls.cause: Only the aggregator is terminal by default

pitfalls.symptom: Answers contradict each other and the user is confused
pitfalls.fix: Add a custom aggregator that reconciles, ranks or votes, and keep a record of the sources

scenarios.title: Pre-merge review of a large change
scenarios.situation: A review bot analyses a diff for security, performance and style. Three specialist agents each take 15 to 40 seconds. Developers will wait about a minute. Quota is ample.
unknowns: Do reviewers need each other's findings?
scenarios.question: Which orchestration?

options.name: Concurrent with a custom aggregator that merges and de-duplicates findings
options.why: Reviewers are independent, so latency is about the slowest (40 seconds) and the aggregator produces one report.
options.tradeoff: Three full model runs in tokens, and an aggregator call to maintain.

options.name: Sequential reviewers
options.why: Latency would be up to 85 seconds with no benefit, since reviewers do not depend on each other.
options.tradeoff: Right if later reviewers should see earlier findings.

options.name: A single reviewer agent covering all three areas
options.tradeoff: Quality in each area may fall, and findings are not separated by role.

flips.then: Limit parallel participants or batch by priority.

flips.if: Reviewers should react to each other

scenarios.takeaway: Concurrent trades tokens for latency when the work is independent.

scenarios.title: Cost-capped FAQ assistant
scenarios.situation: An FAQ assistant answers 50,000 questions a month. A proposal suggests asking three agents each time and voting. The budget has no headroom.
unknowns: Measured error rate of a single agent?
scenarios.question: Do you adopt concurrent voting?

options.name: No: keep one agent, measure errors, and add voting only for question classes where it measurably helps
options.why: Voting triples token cost for every question and the benefit is unproven for low-risk FAQs.
options.tradeoff: You accept the single agent's error rate until the eval proves otherwise.

options.name: Use concurrent voting for every question
options.why: Triple cost with no measured gain.
options.tradeoff: Right for high-stakes answers where one error is expensive.

options.name: Vote only when the first agent reports low confidence
options.why: Spends extra cost only where doubt exists.
options.tradeoff: Needs a reliable confidence signal and a router.

flips.if: Wrong answers carry legal or safety risk
flips.then: Pay for the ensemble and add a reviewer.
Vote on a sample, measure and decide with data.

scenarios.takeaway: Parallel agents multiply cost: buy them with evidence.

quiz.q: Three concurrent agents take 6, 8 and 11 seconds and an aggregator takes 2 seconds. What is the approximate end-to-end time in seconds?
quiz.explain: A concurrent run waits for the slowest participant (11 s), then runs the aggregator (2 s): 13 s. Sequentially the agents alone would take 25 s.

quiz.q: What does the default concurrent aggregator return?
options: One `AgentResponse` with one assistant message per participant
quiz.explain: The default aggregator returns one `AgentResponse` with one assistant message per participant. A custom callback replaces it.

flashcards.front: What bounds latency in a concurrent orchestration?
flashcards.back: The slowest participant plus the aggregator, because of the superstep barrier.

flashcards.front: How do you replace the default aggregation?
flashcards.back: `ConcurrentBuilder(...).with_aggregator(callback)`, which receives the participants' executor responses.

flashcards.front: What is the main cost risk of concurrent runs?
flashcards.back: Cost is the sum of all participants, and parallel calls spike TPM and RPM against quotas.
